H‑Net decides chunk boundaries by learning to place them at whitespace or the start of words in the first stage, and then refining these in the second stage to merge content‑aware units such as whole words or semantic groups . ANSWERABLE: yes

ANSWER: H‑Net decides chunk boundaries by learning to place them at whitespace or the start of words in the first stage, and then refining these in the second stage to merge content‑aware units such as whole words or semantic groups [Q1][Q2][Q3].

question: What is the ratio loss in dynamic chunking and why is it needed?
gold: A loss that guides the fraction of selected boundaries toward a target compression ratio; without it the model could keep everything or compress too much
text:
Evidence: "𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) , 𝑁 −1 𝐹= 1 ∑︁ 𝑏𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1 𝐿 𝐺= 1 ∑︁ 𝑝𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1" [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
Evidence: "where 𝐹 represents the fraction of vectors actually selected, 𝐺 denotes the average boundary probability, and 𝑁 controls the target compression ratio." [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
The ratio loss is defined as 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) , where 𝐹 is the fraction of vectors kept, 𝐺 is the average boundary probability, and 𝑁 sets the desired compression ratio . [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) , 𝑁 −1 𝐹= 1 ∑︁ 𝑏𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1 𝐿 𝐺= 1 ∑︁ 𝑝𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1"  
Q2 [C1] "where 𝐹 represents the fraction of vectors actually selected, 𝐺 denotes the average boundary probability, and 𝑁 controls the target compression ratio."  
Q3 [C2] "Without explicit regularization, the model may converge to trivial solutions: either retaining nearly all vectors (negating computational benefits) or compressing excessively (losing critical information)."  

ANSWER: The ratio loss is defined as 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) [Q1], where 𝐹 is the fraction of vectors kept, 𝐺 is the average boundary probability, and 𝑁 sets the desired compression ratio [Q2]. It is needed to prevent trivial solutions—either keeping almost everything or discarding too much—by guiding the model toward the target compression ratio [Q3].

question: Why did the authors of Attention Is All You Need choose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones?
gold: Both gave nearly identical results; sinusoidal may let the model extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than seen in training
text:
Evidence: "We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos ." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
Evidence: "We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
Evidence: "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
The authors selected sinusoidal positional encodings because they believed the sinusoid form would let the model learn relative positions easily, as offsets become linear functions of the encoding . [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
They also tested learned embeddings and saw almost identical performance, but preferred the sinusoidal version for its potential to extrapolate to longer sequences . [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos ."  
Q2 [C1] "We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))."  
Q3 [C1] "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training."  

ANSWER: The authors selected sinusoidal positional encodings because they believed the sinusoid form would let the model learn relative positions easily, as offsets become linear functions of the encoding [Q1]. They also tested learned embeddings and saw almost identical performance, but preferred the sinusoidal version for its potential to extrapolate to longer sequences [Q2][Q3].

question: What is the Inner Monologue method in Moshi?
gold: Predicting time-aligned text tokens as a prefix to the audio tokens of Moshi's own speech; improves linguistic quality and enables streaming ASR/TTS
text:
Evidence: "Inner Monologue decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens, and predicts this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner." [MOSHI §2 Related Work, p.5]
Evidence: "Not only this “Inner Monologue” method significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech, but we also illustrate how it can provide streaming speech recognition and text-to-speech." [MOSHI p.1]
Evidence: "We moreover show that speech-to-speech generation can be drastically improved by Inner Monologue, a new method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, while remaining compatible with streaming inference." [MOSHI §7 Conclusion, p.41]
The Inner Monologue method in Moshi decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens and predicts them hierarchically, generating text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens . [MOSHI §2 Related Work, p.5]
This improves linguistic quality and enables streaming ASR and TTS . [MOSHI p.1]
It allows speech‑to‑speech generation to be drastically improved while staying compatible with real‑time inference . [MOSHI §7 Conclusion, p.41]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C4] "Inner Monologue decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens, and predicts this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner."  
Q2 [C3] "Not only this “Inner Monologue” method significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech, but we also illustrate how it can provide streaming speech recognition and text-to-speech."  
Q3 [C7] "We moreover show that speech-to-speech generation can be drastically improved by Inner Monologue, a new method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, while remaining compatible with streaming inference."  

ANSWER: The Inner Monologue method in Moshi decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens and predicts them hierarchically, generating text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens [Q1]. This improves linguistic quality and enables streaming ASR and TTS [Q2]. It allows speech‑to‑speech generation to be drastically improved while staying compatible with real‑time inference [Q3].
